The elder's hand rose toward me, palm open, the signal that the rite had begun and that my sealed mouth left only my eyes to warn with. The youth's voice cracked the clearing before I could cross the 
spiralgrass
 to reach her side, and the elder's waiting stare locked on me as the wrong words spilled out. I stepped forward anyway, bare feet pressing into the soft carpet, one hand already lifting to signal the halt I could not speak. The youth's palms flared with unfinished 
Weave-Script
 and the air itself pulled tight around her, heat rushing toward the blank offering she had left unnamed. My pulse slammed against the band at my throat as the warmth drained from her fingers in a visible rush, skin paling to stone while she still held her hands up. I kept moving, closing the distance between the mated-pair trees and the youth before the elder could turn the rite back on me. An elder at the edge shoved both hands forward as if to shove the failure away, and the crowd's silence broke into low murmurs that followed me across the clearing. The youth made a small sound and clenched her fists, but the color stayed gone from her fingertips. The bloodline current moved through the watchers in a single ripple as they tracked my movement instead of the youth's failure. The elder turned fully to me, the demand clear in the open palm he held steady. Julian's gaze did not shift when the second symbol caught the light; he leaned forward instead, one hand braced on the root as if the check he always placed on himself had already begun to slip. The crowd pressed closer, their attention a live weight on my shoulders while the youth's breath came shallow beside me.

My hand tightened around my great-grandmother's old tarot deck. I didn't remember bringing it. I toyed with the idea of letting the cards decide.

The elder’s thumb tapped once against his own wrist, the heat of the clearing thickening against my skin. A rustle at the edge of the 
spiralgrass
 announced the council before they stepped into view—robes catching low branches, boots disturbing the soft carpet where my bare toes still pressed in. The message token rested in the elder’s other hand, its cracked wax seal catching the light in a way that made the clearing feel smaller. I kept my gaze on the youth’s pale hands, but her failure wasn’t the only thing the crowd was watching.

Julian’s voice cut through the murmurs before I could answer. He carried the face of a man striking almost to misshapen before turning gorgeous the longer one looked, tall and gracefully powerful, his dark copper hair wavy and tousled to the nape. Those vivid emerald eyes and the curve of his full lower lip were what her gaze returned to, the small bare notch through one eyebrow the detail she traced in memory.

“You’re asking what I intend?” His tone wasn’t sharp—it was measured, the kind that made sure every word landed exactly where it was meant to. The small bare notch through one eyebrow caught the light as he leaned forward, one hand still braced on the root, the ground steady beneath it.

I swallowed.

“Yes.”

His eyes dropped to my mouth for half a second longer than was polite, the way they always did when he was deciding how much truth to give.

“I intend to keep you from being holed for a crime you didn’t commit.”

The youth made a sound—small, sharp—and clenched her fists. Her thumbnail kept catching on a loose thread at her cuff. The elder’s palm didn’t lower.

“Explain,” he demanded.

Julian didn’t look away from me.

“The token isn’t just a summons. It’s a warning. Someone’s using the bloodline secret to control the current.”

A ripple moved through the watchers—someone gasped, another muttered,

“Fate take it.”

The elder’s gaze flicked to the message token, then back to me.

“You’ve known this?”

I exhaled through my nose.

“Not until now.”

The pulse under my collarbone quickened with the determined set of my jaw, the way it always did when I had to keep speaking even when I wanted to stop. The crowd’s whispers sharpened.

“Then why stand there?” someone called from the back. “Why not act?”

Julian’s fingers tightened around the root.

“Because the only way to stop it is to let the secret surface.”

Silence. The air drawn taut. The elder’s palm finally lowered, but his eyes stayed on me.

“And if we refuse to let it?”

Julian’s voice dropped.

“Then the secret surfaces anyway. And someone dies.”

The youth’s breath hitched. The air in the clearing went still.

I held my ground.

“We don’t have a choice.”

The elder exhaled through his nose, slow and deliberate.

“Fine. But first—” His gaze flicked to Julian. “You’ll answer one question.”

Julian’s expression didn’t change.

“Ask.”

“Why protect her?” The elder’s palm hovered between us, as if measuring the distance. “What do you gain?”

Julian’s ring finger dragged once along the bark before he answered.

“Because I’ve seen what happens when secrets are buried.”

The youth’s small sound came again. Her knuckles stayed locked around the edge of her sleeve.

The elder’s palm lowered at last.

“Then let it surface.”

The air in the clearing eased with his breath. The message token passed from hand to hand, the murmurs growing sharper. The bloodline secret, once only a ripple, now moved through the watchers like open suspicion.

I realized the old tarot deck was still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slipped out—the ink at the bottom edge shifted as my thumb passed over it.

I sent my plea into the turning weave.

“Tempt Fate.”

Grandma never let me play with that one. A sword raised to a blood-red sky, lightning arcing down from the clouds (or maybe arcing up?) Ow! Static shock reminds me I need to pay attention to the present…

I realize the deck is still in my hand. As I slide Petition Fate back in, I notice a flash of red in the otherwise gold stack. "Tempt Fate." Ow!

The stone circle shimmered with magic, its runes flaring in answer to the weight of oaths spoken too near its edge. Thorne stepped fully into the light, his silver-threaded cloak drawing the glow inward along each thread. His boot scraped once against the rune-carved edge.

"You've carried this bloodline shadow long enough," he said, voice low and edged with ritual finality. "The Alignment Reading will not hold if the fracture is not named. Speak the truth, or the vow-bond ends here."

A faint resin scent rose from the disturbed root as Julian straightened. The notch in his brow caught the light as he angled his body slightly between Thorne and me.

"She owes you nothing," he answered, calm but already set in the line of his shoulders.

My pulse tightened at the base of my throat.

"This cannot occur."

Thorne did not blink.

"It already has." He reached into his robe and withdrew a folded parchment sealed with the council's iron sigil. The wax gleamed wetly under the runes. He extended it to Julian without ceremony.

"The council requires your presence for questioning regarding the artifact incident and the bond's instability. Refusal will be treated as obstruction."

Julian took the summons, fingers closing around the edge. The paper whispered against his skin. For a breath he studied the seal, then lifted his eyes to mine again. The look held no demand, only the steady invitation to decide what came next.

The runes pulsed once, brighter, as the circle itself marked the shift.

The stone circle hummed beneath my feet, the runes pulsing, their light drawing the moisture from the air into a haze that clung to everything. Thorne's cloak caught the glow and funneled it inward, the threads drawing the power from the earth. His boot scraped against the rune-carved edge again, the sound sharp enough to lift the fine hairs on my forearms in a single ripple.

The sealed parchment in Julian's hand whispered against his skin as he lowered it. The wax seal was still damp, the council’s iron sigil glistening. He didn’t look at me. His eyes stayed fixed on Thorne, on the way the Arbiter’s fingers tapped against the stone in a rhythm that wasn’t quite a heartbeat. Something in the set of Julian’s shoulders made the muscle under my left eye jump—he was bracing himself. Not for the summons, but for whatever came after.

I should have known then. A choice like this doesn’t come without teeth.

"Fine," I said, stepping forward before Thorne could press his advantage. "I’ll accept the consequences. Whatever they are." My voice didn’t shake. That was the first cost.

The council’s whispers sharpened into something uglier. A woman in the front row—her face a map of lines that had seen too much sun—leaned toward the man beside her and muttered something about bloodlines and debts. I caught the word *kwishif* on her lips, the scholar’s term for the Eight-born, and my fingers tightened around the pendant at my throat. The one my mother had given me the day she left. The one I’d stopped wearing after the first time someone spat the word *kwishif* at me like a curse.

Thorne’s lips curled. "Good. Then you’ll answer for the artifact incident *and* the bond’s instability. Both." His gaze flicked to Julian, then back to me. "The council requires your presence for questioning *immediately*." The emphasis on *immediately* pressed between my ribs.

Julian’s ring finger twitched against the parchment. The motion was small—a grounding thing, I’d learned—but it was enough to make the roof of my mouth go dry. I’d seen that hand steady itself against a wall, against my waist, against the small of my back when the world tilted. Now it was holding a summons that would drag me before a tribunal that had already decided my guilt.

"If this is the price," I said, "I’ll pay it."

The words tasted like ash. The council’s murmurs died. Even Thorne paused, his fingers hovering over the next question. I’d expected resistance, deflection, a counter-offer. Not this.

Julian exhaled, slow and controlled, bracing for a blow he wasn’t sure he could take. His eyes locked onto mine. Not with warmth. Not with accusation.

With *relief*.

The metal edge of the pendant caught on the inside of my collarbone. The cost wasn’t just the summons. It was the way his relief made me question everything I thought I knew about what this meant, about what I was supposed to feel.

Thorne’s voice cut through the silence. "Then it’s settled." He extended a hand toward me, palm up, as if expecting me to step into an unspoken trap. "Come now. The chamber awaits."

I didn’t move. The stone circle’s energy pulsed again, the runes flaring brighter, and for a heartbeat I swore I felt Julian’s gaze on the back of my neck. The pendant at my throat—my mother’s—felt heavier than the tarot deck in my pocket, heavier than the secrets coiled in my ribs.

The cost wasn’t just the questioning. It was the way my body remembered the weight of his hand on my waist. The way my heel lifted half an inch from the stone when his voice dropped lower than it should. The way I’d just vowed to walk into a trap, and all I could think about was how his fingers had steadied themselves against the parchment like they were steadying themselves against me.

I swallowed. "Lead the way."

The pendant didn’t burn anymore. It was ice against my skin.

But just as I prepared to step forward, a shadow fell over the chamber, and the air thickened with an unspoken threat. Vow Arbiter Thorne loomed closer, his presence a chilling reminder of the power he wielded. I could feel the weight of his scrutiny, a silent promise that my past would not remain buried for long.
A.action: I make a choice that costs me something.
A.dialogue: If this is the price, I'll pay it.

The runes pulsed beneath our feet like a living vein, cold and insistent. Julian’s emerald eyes darkened as my words settled, his full lower lip tightening into that almost-smile, a blend of wounding intent and verification. He turned the ring on his finger once, the metal flashing in the dim light, then closed his fingers around the token still warm from my palm.

“Prove it,” I said, my voice low and firm. “Immediately.”

He did not respond right away. The crowd’s whispers sharpened, Thorne’s gaze a dagger at our backs. Julian stepped closer, his tall frame blocking the worst of the stares, the powerful grace of his shoulders forming a shield I hadn’t sought. His mouth brushed the shell of my ear.

“I already have,” he murmured, the words heavy with a geas unspoken. “The artifact is yours if you desire it. But if I take it now, the council will mark me for it. Say the word, and I walk away. Say nothing, and I bear the cost.”

My breath caught. The token between us was no longer cool metal; it had transformed into a live wire of magical binding I could not retract. He waited, the notch through his brow stark in the rune-light, every line of him both offering and daring me to refuse. I remained silent.

As I leaned forward into the space between us, the strong, frank face that made the circle track its every shift before they could stop themselves changed with the choice I held, though I kept my eyes on the token as if their notice were incidental. The deep auburn waves that had once pulled his words off course caught the rune-light he had already claimed.

Julian’s hand turned the ring once more. Then he drew the artifact from beneath his cloak—the small, carved thing that could unravel both our bloodlines—and slipped it into the folds of his own garment. His gaze held mine a heartbeat longer than safety allowed. He turned and walked toward the edge of the stone circle, the crowd parting before the quiet certainty of his stride. The runes flared once, colder still, as if marking the choice we had both made. Thorne’s voice rose behind us, sharp with triumph. Julian did not look back. The weight of what he now carried settled between my ribs like a second heart.

The moment shattered.

Thorne stepped forward, his presence an undeniable force, the Vow Arbiter's authority crackling in the air.

"You think you can escape the consequences of your choice?" he challenged, his voice echoing with the weight of ancient power. The crowd fell silent, the tension thickening as they awaited his next move, the stakes of our entangled fates rising with each heartbeat.
A.action: I test whether I can trust him with everything.

The stone circle hummed beneath my feet, each pulse of the runes landing against the soles of my boots before I could brace for it. The air smelled of damp earth and the sharp metallic tang of the council's meddling. Thorne stood at the circle’s edge, his silver-threaded cloak catching the eerie glow and drawing it toward him in steady lines. His boot scraped against the rune-carved stone again, the sound cutting through the tense silence and leaving the air thinner in its wake. He didn’t look at me. His gaze stayed fixed on Julian, on the way the Arbiter’s fingers tapped against the parchment in his hand—a rhythm that wasn’t quite steady. Something in the set of Julian’s shoulders made my stomach tighten. He was bracing himself. Not for the summons. For whatever came after.

I swallowed the taste of ash in my mouth.

"I don’t want your help," I said, stepping forward before Thorne could press his advantage. "I want the truth. All of it. Without your interference."

Julian’s heel lifted once, the sole peeling from the stone with a faint tack. A grounding thing, I’d learned. But in that moment, it looked like his weight had shifted onto the heel that still touched stone. His eyes flickered up, catching mine, and for a heartbeat, the runes’ hum dropped to a single low note that vibrated in my molars. Not with warmth. Not with accusation. With relief. The relief settled into the lines around his eyes.

Thorne’s smirk rose, the air around his mouth seeming to thin.

"Truth?" He spread his hands, the cloak’s threads shifting with the motion. "You’ll find it’s a heavy thing, girl. One many have tried to lift—and none have walked away unbroken."

Julian’s next breath caught on the inhale, a thin whistle through his teeth. The wax seal glistened, untouched.

"You don’t have to go in there," he said, his voice low. Not a command. A plea. "Not like this."

I turned my back on Thorne and faced Julian fully. The runes’ light caught the curve of his jaw, the faint scar through his eyebrow.

"You think I’m afraid?" I asked, tilting my chin up. "You think I’ll break before they do?"

His collar shifted as he swallowed, the fabric whispering once against his throat. A flicker. A hesitation. Then his lashes lifted, and his expression shuttered.

"I think you’re standing in a room full of people who would tear you apart for the things you’ve buried." A drop of wax slid from the seal and landed on the back of his wrist, cooling to a pale bead. "And I think you’re about to hand them the blade."

Thorne chuckled, a dry, brittle sound.

"Well said, Arbiter. But the girl’s made her choice." His fingers hovered over the next rune, waiting. "Let’s see how long she lasts."

Julian’s jaw set. He stepped between me and Thorne, blocking the Arbiter’s advance.

"You don’t get to decide that for her."

I reached out, my fingers brushing Julian’s wrist. The contact grounded me.

"I do," I said softly. "Because this is my secret to uncover. My cost to pay." I stepped forward, pressing closer to Julian, my voice dropping to a whisper only he could hear. "And I’m not afraid of the truth. Are you?"

He went still. Not because I’d challenged him. Because for the first time in a long time, someone had given him a reason to stand his ground. Neither of you speaks.
A.action: I walk into the danger instead of away from it.

The stone circle pulsed underfoot, the runes flaring in a rhythm that matched the air’s slow pull. Thorne’s silver-threaded cloak caught the glow and funneled it inward, the threads drinking the power from the earth. His boot scraped the rune-carved edge again, the sound sharp enough to make the fine hairs on my forearms rise in a single ripple. The sealed parchment in Julian’s hand whispered against his skin as he lowered it. The wax seal was still damp, the council’s iron sigil glistening. His eyes stayed fixed on Thorne, on the way the Arbiter’s fingers tapped the stone in a rhythm that wasn’t quite a heartbeat. Something in the set of Julian’s shoulders made the muscle under my left eye jump—he was bracing, not for the summons, but for whatever came after.

I should have known then. A choice like this doesn’t come without teeth.

“Fine,” I said, stepping forward before Thorne could press his advantage. “I’ll accept the consequences. Whatever they are.”

My voice didn’t shake. That was the first cost.

The council’s whispers sharpened into something uglier. A woman in the front row—her face a map of lines that had seen too much sun—leaned toward the man beside her and muttered something about bloodlines and debts. I caught the word *kwishif* on her lips, the scholar’s term for the Eight-born, and my thumbnail found the dented edge of the pendant and traced it once. The one my mother had given me the day she left. The one I’d stopped wearing after the first time someone spat the word *kwishif* at me like a curse.

Thorne’s lips curled. “Good. Then you’ll answer for the artifact incident *and* the bond’s instability. Both.”

His gaze flicked to Julian, then back to me. “The council requires your presence for questioning *immediately*.”

The emphasis on *immediately* pressed between my ribs. Julian’s ring finger twitched against the parchment. The motion was small—a grounding thing, I’d learned—but it was enough to make the roof of my mouth go dry. I’d seen that hand steady itself against a wall, against my waist, against the small of my back when the world tilted. Now it was holding a summons that would drag me before a tribunal that had already decided my guilt.

“If this is the price,” I said, “I’ll pay it.”

The words left a grit of old chalk on my tongue.

The council’s murmurs died. Even Thorne paused, his fingers hovering over the next question. I’d expected resistance, deflection, a counter-offer. Not this.

Julian exhaled, slow and controlled, bracing for a blow he wasn’t sure he could take. His eyes locked onto mine. Not with warmth. Not with accusation. With *relief*.

The metal edge of the pendant caught on the inside of my collarbone. The cost wasn’t just the summons. It was the way his relief made me question everything I thought I knew about what this meant, about what I was supposed to feel.

Thorne’s voice cut through the silence. “Then it’s settled.”

He extended a hand toward me, palm up, as if expecting me to step into an unspoken trap. “Come now. The chamber awaits.”

I didn’t move.

The stone circle exhaled a draft of cold air that lifted the hem of my coat and carried the smell of wet iron. The chain of the pendant slid a cold inch lower against my sternum with each breath.

The cost wasn’t just the questioning. It was the way my body remembered the weight of his hand on my waist. The way my heel lifted half an inch from the stone when his voice dropped lower than it should. The way I’d just vowed to walk into a trap, and all I could think about was how the parchment edge had bent under the same two fingertips he’d once pressed to the inside of my wrist.

I swallowed.

“Lead the way.”

The pendant didn’t burn anymore. It was ice against my skin.

But just as I prepared to step forward, a shadow fell over the chamber, and the air thickened with an unspoken threat.

Vow Arbiter Thorne loomed closer, his presence a chilling reminder of the power he wielded. I could feel the weight of his scrutiny, a silent promise that my past would not remain buried for long. The room goes quiet.
A.action: I let him see how much it hurt.
A.dialogue: You don't get to disappear and come back like nothing happened.

He didn’t even shift his weight—just stood there, the parchment crumpling slightly under his grip. His thumb pressed once against the parchment seam, flattening it.

The council’s whispers sharpened into something uglier, a woman near the front muttering something about *kwishif*—the Eight-born—and my fingers clenched into fists. My mother’s pendant had been a warning. A reminder. A secret.

The offer waited between us. Protection. A cage. A transaction. Julian’s heel lifted half an inch from the stone, then settled again. He didn’t speak. He didn’t need to. A single breath left him through his nose, measured and quiet.

I swallowed. It was ice.

"Lead the way," I said. Neither of you speaks.
A.action: I make the move I've been afraid to make.

A child’s bare foot scraped once against the stone floor, the sound sharp under the rising voices, the slant of light through its threads catching flecks of gold that shifted with the threads. I held my ground, shoulders set, but the loose braid at my nape caught the breeze, strands catching against the curve of my neck. The silver ring on my finger pressed into my skin, carrying the weight of the past I had not chosen.

I slid the petition card back in without drawing it, the motion practiced, the card’s edges still damp where my thumb had rested. A flash of red glinted between the gold stack. Temptation. The story watched the light along my throat brighten. Julian’s name moved through the murmurs again, low and edged, a reminder that any word I spoke here would travel farther than intended.

B.dialogue: I'm done waiting for it to come to me.

B.text:
The veil-canopy shuddered above us, its golden threads catching torchlight in broken patterns. The crowd’s fury pressed in, a living thing that smelled of iron and old vows. My throat burned with everything I had swallowed for years, and before I could stop myself I turned to Julian, the words tearing free.

“You left after the binding, and I carried the fracture alone. It was like offering my name to the moons and watching them take it without answer.”

He stood close enough that the heat of him cut through the chill 
the Fold
 always sent along the Verge. His hand rose, thumb and forefinger turning the signet ring at his knuckle in that slow, unconscious motion that always made my chest tighten. Amber eyes held mine, unreadable, the grey streak in his dark hair catching the light like a scar that had never quite healed. Broad shoulders filled the space between us, steady where everything else tilted. The Elder’s staff scraped once, a small sound lost under the crowd. Julian’s gaze flicked to the damp page still crumpled in my fist, then back to me—something raw and unspoken arcing between us, thin as the breath before a wish answers.

The crowd surged closer, their voices sharpening into accusations, a blade of sound. Julian’s ring turned again, metal flashing once in warning. He leaned in, his breath a blade’s edge against my ear.

“Then tell me what you paid when the bond refused to break.”

The veil above us rippled, a single thread snapping free and drifting down between us like a severed oath, a ghost of promises broken. The torches guttered, their flames bending toward the distant basin as if 
the Fold
 itself had leaned in to listen to the words we had finally spoken aloud.

The moment shattered. Something yanked them back to reality—a sound, a hesitation, the world refusing to wait.

As the tension crackled between us, I felt the weight of time pressing down, reminding me of the Alignment Circle's next reading cycle looming ahead. The knowledge that our fractured vow-bond would soon be exposed intensified the air around us, and I knew we had little time left to confront the truth of our feelings before the world demanded its reckoning. For a second, everything stops.
B.action: I let him see how much it hurt.
B.dialogue: You don't get to disappear and come back like nothing happened.

B.text:
The veil-canopy shuddered again, its frayed edges catching the air in short, uneven pulls. The crowd’s shouts rose, their jeers pressing against the ancient sigils carved into the stone beneath my feet—sigils that should have held, but now shifted under the lie that had been spoken. I tightened my grip on the page still damp from my thumb, the ink bleeding slightly as I folded it smaller, smaller, until only the corner remained visible. The Elder’s staff thudded against the ground, the carved runes along its length flaring faintly as the wood took the impact. His breath hitched, stale with something bitter—sacrifice-leaf, or the truth he wouldn’t speak.

Julian stepped from the shadows, the movement so fluid the darkness held its shape around him a moment longer. His left heel dragged once across the stone, the scrape cutting through the crowd noise before he planted it again.

“You don’t have to do this alone,” he said, his voice low enough that only I would hear it over the crowd’s roar. A faint click came from the ring on his smallest finger whenever it struck the seam of his trousers.

I exhaled through my nose, the sound too controlled, too deliberate.

“Assistance is the easy way out,” I said, my voice steady despite the damp collar clinging to my throat. “I didn’t come here to compromise.” The corner of the page pressed into my skin, the damp half-moon a stark reminder of how much I’d already given up to get this far. The crowd’s anger thickened, their voices pressing harder against the walls.

Julian’s gaze didn’t waver.

“Then tell me what you need,” he said, the words settling into the space the last torch pop had left. His shoulders dropped a fraction, the shift pulling the hem of his coat taut across his back. “Because I can see the cost of what you’re carrying. And I’m not letting you bear it.” The stillness lands.
B.action: I make the move I've been afraid to make.
B.dialogue: I'm tired of pretending I don't feel this.

B.text:
The veil-canopy above us trembled, its fabric brushing the nape of my neck as I advanced. The Elder’s staff rasped against the stone, the carved sigils flaring once—an omen, a challenge, or perhaps both. His breath carried the stale scent of sacrifice-leaf, the air thick and almost palpable. Around us, the crowd’s murmurs surged into a tumult, bodies pressing closer, the atmosphere saturated with sweat and the weight of ancient ink.

Julian lingered half a step behind, his form taut, fingers tapping a silent rhythm against his thigh—the subtle tell of his rapt attention. His squinting eyes caught the torchlight, the left lid twitching as he tracked the Elder’s movements.

“You stall what fate demands,” the Elder intoned, his voice low and deliberate. “Step aside or name your price.”

I clenched the hem of my sleeve, the tarot deck’s weight a quiet promise against my ribs. “I do not seek your aid,” I replied, my voice unwavering despite the heat rising in my cheeks. “I seek the truth.”

The crowd’s fury thickened, the air heavy with arcane binding and something sharper: doubt. Julian’s heel lifted momentarily before settling flat. The Elder’s staff wavered, the sigils flickering as the light dimmed. “This changes nothing,” he asserted, though the words felt hollow.

I stepped closer, the damp stone beneath my boots now brushing against the toes of his. “It changes everything,” I countered. “And you are aware of it.”

The folded corner of the page pressed a damp half-moon into my skin. The torches flared, their light intensifying against the edges of the circle. The circle held as doubt took root. The Elder’s grip faltered, yet the crowd’s skepticism solidified. A ripple coursed through the gathering, bodies shifting forward as the space constricted.

Someone hissed my family’s name, another spat *misalignment*, and the torches flickered, their flames shrinking to blue pinpoints.

Julian’s left hand settled against the small of my back, a deliberate claim that shifted the air between us. “Then let her speak,” he urged, his voice calm yet laced with a darker undercurrent. “Or admit you fear what unfolds when she does.”

The room goes quiet.
B.action: I face the consequence I've been dreading.
B.dialogue: Whatever happens next, I did this with my eyes open.

B.text:
The veil-canopy rustled, the fabric whispering against itself, and the air inside the circle thickened with the scent of sweat and old incense. My fingers curled into the damp edge of the tarot deck where it rested against my ribs, the weight of the cards a promise I wasn’t sure I could keep. The Elder stood too close—his breath stale with sacrifice-leaf, his left sandal scraping sideways through a puddle, once, twice—before he straightened, the carved sigils along his staff flaring faintly in time with the restless shifting of the crowd. Around us, the shouts rose again, voices pressing against the circle’s boundary, and the heat of their anger pressed against my ribs until my breath caught.

“You stall what fate demands,” the Elder said, his voice low and deliberate, the words settling over the murmurs.

I didn’t look away from the page still clutched in my hand, the edges damp where my thumb had lingered. “If this is the price, I’ll pay it.”

His staff’s iron ferrule scraped stone, the sigils brightening as the crowd’s murmur drew into one low, dangerous sound. A shift passed through the gathering, bodies pressing forward until the circle’s edge checked them. Someone hissed my family’s name, another spat *misalignment*, and the torches flickered, their light dimming for a heartbeat. In that flicker, the Elder’s control slipped—a fraction of a sag in his shoulders, the weight of the staff pulling him down. My heel stayed planted against the stone. “You’re reading the absence of evidence,” I said, “and calling it alignment.”

The Elder’s mouth opened, then closed. A tendon jumped in his neck as his gaze tracked the page, a corner folded under his stare. The crowd’s anger thickened, the air heavy with arcane binding and something sharper: doubt. His fingers trembled on the staff, betraying him. “This changes nothing.”

I stepped closer, the space between us narrowing until only a breath remained. “It changes everything,” I said. “And you know it.”

The torches flared, their light pressing harder against the edges of the circle. The circle held as doubt settled into the spaces between them. The Elder’s grip was faltering, yet the crowd’s skepticism held firm. I stepped back, my body moving before thought could catch up.

Then Julian stepped out of the shadows. Neither of you speaks.
B.action: I refuse to be anyone's secret.
B.dialogue: If you want me, you want all of it. In the open.

B.text:
The veil-canopy shivered above me, its gold-threaded fabric shifting where a current of air passed beneath it, the weight of the afternoon pressing the air against my skin. The Elder’s staff scraped stone again, the carved sigils along its length flaring faintly in answer to the crowd’s movement. His gaze pinned me where I stood, his breath stale with the bitter tang of sacrifice-leaf.

“This cannot continue,” he said, low and deliberate.

“Name your price. Or step aside.”

I curled my fingers deeper into the fabric of my sleeve, the page’s inked edge rasping against the callus on my thumb.

“I’ll pay it,” I said, not a question. Not a negotiation.

“But not with what you’re offering.”

My nail caught on a frayed thread of the page, the edge lifting the skin along my knuckle. Behind me, the crowd’s murmurs thickened into a low, hungry sound, bodies pressing forward until the circle’s edge checked them. I didn’t look away.

His mouth opened, then closed. A tendon jumped in his neck as his gaze tracked the page, the edges still smudged from my thumb’s rest.

“You stall what fate demands,” he said again, the words leaving a cut of silence between us.

“Name your price.”

“I’ve already named it,” I said.

“Truth.”

Ink from the page left a faint smear across the pad of my thumb. The circle held as doubt took root. The Elder’s grip was faltering, yet the crowd’s skepticism solidified. The page edge lifted and settled against my wrist with each breath.

“You know it changes everything,” I said.

“And you know it.”

The crowd’s shouts rose again, a wave of dissent that wanted blood, not answers. The Elder’s left sandal scraped sideways through a puddle—once, twice—before he straightened. He exhaled through his nose, the decision already fixed in the set of his jaw.

“Then tell me what you’re hiding,” he said.

“Or leave.”

The sigils along his staff pulsed once, brighter than before. The veil-canopy swayed overhead, its rustling fabric amplifying the crowd’s unrest. I tilted my head slightly, listening for the one thing I needed most: the sound of footsteps approaching from the shadows behind him. The room goes quiet.
B.action: I force the confrontation to a head.

B.text:
A drop of condensation fell from the canopy's edge and struck the stone between us. The hem of my cloak brushed my wrist, the fibers coarse under my skin where I’d twisted the fabric into a fist. Around me, the crowd’s shouts rose in waves, a tide of voices that wanted blood instead of answers. The Elder’s staff scraped stone again, the iron ferrule pressing into the ground until the vibration reached my feet. He didn’t take his eyes off me, but his breath hitched, stale with sacrifice-leaf.

“Twice now,” he murmured, “you’ve stood between us and what fate decrees.”

I exhaled through my nose, slow and measured. The damp page still clutched in my hand bent at the seam, the ink blurred where my thumb had pressed.

“I’m not here to name prices,” I said. “I’m here to find the truth.”

His left sandal scuffed sideways through a puddle—once, twice—before he straightened. The torchlight caught the lines around his mouth, deepening as he flicked a glance at the restless crowd. Someone hissed my family’s name. Another spat *misalignment*. The torches flickered, their light stuttering for a heartbeat. In that flicker, the Elder’s left sandal scraped once more against the wet stone. His shoulders sagged, the weight of the iron pulling him down. I didn’t look away.

“You’re reading absence,” I said, “and calling it alignment.”

The Elder’s mouth opened, then closed. A tendon leapt in his neck as his gaze dropped to the page—edges catching on the ridge of my knuckle. The crowd’s anger thickened, the air heavy with arcane binding and something sharper: doubt. His fingers trembled on the staff.

“This changes nothing,” he lied.

I stepped closer until the space between us narrowed to a breath.

“It changes everything,” I said. “And you know it.”

The folded corner of the page pressed a damp half-moon into my skin. The torches flared, pressing harder against the edges of the circle. The Elder’s heel lifted once, then settled again. I stepped back, my body moving before thought could catch up.

A shadow shifted at the edge of the canopy. Julian stepped into the flickering torchlight, his black hair catching the glow, the distinctive streak of grey cutting through it in a clean line. His amber eyes met mine, unhurried and assessing. The crowd’s murmurs stilled, not just from his presence, but from the way attention gathered around him and held. He didn’t ask permission. He didn’t wait for an invitation. He simply stepped forward, close enough that the scent of him—warm with old paper and distant fires—filled the narrowing space between us.

“You’re going to tell them everything,” he said, low and deliberate. His left hand rested on the hilt of a blade I hadn’t noticed before, the leather worn smooth by use. “Or I will.”

A single thread snapped loose from the canopy and drifted down between us. Neither of you speaks.
B.action: I stand at the threshold of the decision that changes everything.
